description: Team TerraSignal is a technology-focused team competing in NASA Space Apps Challenge: “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” Led by Sarujan Puvirajan, a Cybersecurity & Software Engineer and MSc Cybersecurity student at the University of Hertfordshire. We are building SAT-SCOPE, an AI platform combining satellite temperature, vegetation, precipitation, and fire data to detect and explain trends and anomalies.
summary:
Terra Signal is an interactive Earth observation and environmental anomaly detection platform developed to address NASA Space Apps Challenge’s “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. It transforms historical NASA POWER data into meaningful insights about temperature, precipitation, and soil wetness changes across the globe.

Our platform analyzes 15 years of environmental observations (2011–2025) across 615 geographic grid locations, enabling users to explore historical patterns through interactive maps, time-series charts, and statistical anomaly detection. We developed four country-specific Isolation Forest machine-learning models for Australia, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States to identify unusual combinations of environmental conditions.

Terra Signal combines statistical methods, machine learning, and geographic visualization to make complex Earth science data accessible and understandable. Users can investigate environmental changes, compare regions, and identify potential climate-related risks without requiring advanced technical expertise.

The project is important because understanding environmental variability can support climate awareness, agricultural planning, drought monitoring, and informed decision-making. By transforming NASA’s open scientific data into an accessible analytical platform, Terra Signal empowers researchers, communities, and decision-makers to better understand our changing planet.
details:
Terra Signal – Intelligent Earth System Monitoring and Environmental Anomaly Detection

Project Overview

Terra Signal is an interactive environmental monitoring and analysis platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge’s “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. Our project combines NASA Earth science data, statistical analysis, machine learning, and geographic visualization to help users understand environmental changes and identify unusual conditions across different regions of the world.

The platform transforms complex historical environmental observations into accessible visual insights, allowing users to investigate temperature, precipitation, and soil wetness through an interactive web-based dashboard.

What Does Terra Signal Do?

Terra Signal enables users to explore 15 years of historical environmental observations, covering 2011–2025, using NASA POWER data collected across 615 global land-grid locations. The historical archive contains approximately 110,700 monthly location records.

Users can select countries and geographic regions, explore historical environmental measurements, examine time-series charts, and identify anomalies relative to historical seasonal conditions.

The platform focuses on three environmental indicators:

  • Temperature: Identifies unusually high or low temperatures using historical seasonal averages and Z-score analysis.
  • Precipitation: Detects unusually dry or wet conditions using historical rainfall percentile analysis.
  • Soil wetness: Measures deviations from historical soil wetness conditions to identify potential environmental moisture stress.

In addition to individual environmental indicators, Terra Signal uses machine learning to identify compound anomalies, where multiple environmental variables exhibit unusual behavior simultaneously.

How Does the System Work?

The system follows a structured analytical pipeline consisting of data acquisition, preprocessing, statistical analysis, machine-learning inference, and visualization.

1. Data Acquisition and Preparation

We use NASA POWER historical environmental data, including near-surface air temperature (T2M), corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), and root-zone soil wetness (GWETROOT).

The data is organized by geographic location, year, and month. During preprocessing, invalid observations are handled, environmental variables are standardized into consistent analytical features, and historical seasonal baselines are calculated.

Geographic boundary datasets enable the platform to associate environmental observations with countries and administrative regions.

2. Statistical Environmental Analysis

Terra Signal applies three statistical techniques to identify environmental anomalies:

  • Z-score analysis: Measures how far an observed temperature deviates from its historical seasonal mean.
  • Percentage deviation: Quantifies changes in soil wetness relative to historical conditions.
  • Percentile analysis: Determines whether precipitation is unusually high or low compared with historical observations.

These methods provide interpretable results that help users understand the environmental conditions contributing to detected anomalies.

3. Machine-Learning-Based Compound Anomaly Detection

We developed four country-specific Isolation Forest models for Australia, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Isolation Forest is an unsupervised machine-learning algorithm that identifies unusual observations by isolating them through randomized decision trees. Unlike supervised classification, it does not require manually labelled environmental anomaly examples.

Each model integrates three environmental features: temperature Z-score, soil wetness deviation, and a transformed rainfall percentile feature.

The models were developed using a chronological data split:

  • 2011–2020: Historical seasonal baseline calculation.
  • 2021–2023: Machine-learning training.
  • 2024–2025: Independent holdout evaluation.

We used StandardScaler for feature normalization and trained each Isolation Forest with 200 estimators, an 8% contamination setting, and a fixed random seed of 42 to support reproducibility.

Across the four countries, the models were trained using 3,312 observations and evaluated using 2,208 held-out observations.

The trained models are saved as reusable Joblib files and integrated into the backend, allowing the application to perform predictions without retraining the models whenever users access the dashboard.

For other countries with available historical observations, Terra Signal supports statistical environmental analysis and, where sufficient spatial observations exist, on-demand spatial anomaly detection. The system distinguishes these results from predictions produced by the four independently trained historical models.

4. Interactive Visualization

The frontend presents environmental information through an interactive geographic dashboard. Users can explore different regions, inspect environmental measurements, visualize historical changes, and investigate anomaly detection results.

The backend processes geographic selections, retrieves historical observations, calculates statistical features, and applies the appropriate anomaly detection method.

This architecture makes scientific data more accessible while maintaining transparency about the source of observations and the analytical methods used.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Terra Signal is designed to reduce the technical barriers associated with accessing and interpreting Earth science data.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Climate awareness: Helping communities and students understand historical environmental variability and changing conditions.
  • Agricultural planning: Providing insights into rainfall deficits, soil moisture conditions, and potential environmental stress.
  • Environmental monitoring: Supporting the identification of unusual temperature, precipitation, and soil wetness patterns.
  • Research and education: Providing an accessible platform for exploring NASA environmental datasets and machine-learning applications.
  • Regional comparison: Allowing users to investigate environmental differences across countries and geographic regions.
  • Data-driven decision-making: Providing interpretable environmental information that may support further scientific investigation and planning.

The intended impact is to make Earth science information more accessible, understandable, and useful to a wider audience. Rather than requiring users to download large datasets and develop their own analytical tools, Terra Signal brings environmental observations and anomaly detection together within a unified interface.

The platform is intended as an exploratory scientific decision-support tool, not a replacement for professional weather forecasting, disaster warning systems, or validated climate risk assessments.

Technologies, Tools, and Development Environment

Terra Signal was developed using open-source technologies and publicly available Earth science datasets.

Frontend

  • React: Development of the interactive user interface.
  • JavaScript: Frontend application logic and data processing.
  • Vite: Frontend development and build tooling.
  • HTML and CSS: Interface structure, styling, and responsive presentation.
  • Geographic visualization and charting tools: Interactive maps, historical charts, and environmental data visualization.

Backend and Machine Learning

  • Python: Data processing, statistical analysis, and machine-learning implementation.
  • FastAPI: REST API development and communication between the frontend and backend.
  • Uvicorn: Application server for running the FastAPI backend.
  • Pandas: Historical dataset processing and tabular analysis.
  • NumPy: Numerical operations and environmental feature calculations.
  • SciPy: Scientific and statistical computations.
  • Scikit-learn: Isolation Forest model training, feature scaling, and anomaly detection.
  • Joblib: Saving and loading trained machine-learning models.

Development and Reproducibility

  • Jupyter Notebook: Data exploration, model development, evaluation, and reproducible training workflows.
  • Git and GitHub: Source code management, version control, and project collaboration.
  • Python virtual environments: Dependency isolation and consistent execution.
  • Automated backend testing: Verification of model inference, historical data processing, and application functionality.

The project was developed and tested using conventional personal computing hardware. Because Isolation Forest is computationally efficient, the system does not require specialized GPU hardware or expensive computing infrastructure.

Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of Terra Signal lies in combining multiple environmental indicators into a unified, interpretable anomaly detection system rather than displaying environmental measurements independently.

Traditional environmental dashboards often focus on visualizing individual variables. Terra Signal extends this approach by examining relationships between temperature, rainfall, and soil wetness to identify unusual combinations of environmental conditions.

For example, a region experiencing unusually high temperatures, low rainfall, and reduced soil wetness may exhibit compound environmental stress. Terra Signal allows users to investigate these conditions together through statistical indicators and machine-learning anomaly scores.

Another innovative aspect is the combination of global historical exploration with country-specific trained models. This approach provides broad geographic accessibility while enabling more specialized historical analysis for selected countries.

The project also emphasizes explainability. Users can investigate the individual environmental indicators contributing to an anomaly rather than relying exclusively on a machine-learning prediction.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors throughout the design and implementation process:

Scientific reliability: We prioritized real NASA environmental observations and removed simulated datasets from the final implementation to avoid misleading scientific interpretations.

Seasonal variability: Environmental conditions differ across seasons and geographic regions. Historical monthly baselines allow observations to be compared with appropriate seasonal reference conditions.

Data quality and availability: We considered missing observations, geographic coverage, and the limitations of coarse spatial resolution. Regions without sufficient observations are handled without inventing environmental measurements.

Machine-learning suitability: Isolation Forest was selected because labelled environmental anomaly datasets were not available and the algorithm supports efficient unsupervised anomaly detection.

Reproducibility: We preserved the historical datasets, training scripts, executed Jupyter notebooks, model configurations, and trained model files so that the analytical results can be independently reproduced.

Evaluation integrity: We used chronological training and testing periods to reduce temporal data leakage and evaluated models using previously unseen observations.

Accessibility and usability: We designed the platform to make complex environmental information understandable through maps, charts, and interpretable statistical indicators.

Computational efficiency: The application uses lightweight statistical methods and pre-trained machine-learning models, reducing computational requirements during dashboard interaction.

Transparency and limitations: We distinguish measured environmental observations from calculated anomalies, historical model inference from on-demand spatial analysis, and anomaly rates from classification accuracy.

Current Limitations and Future Development

The current implementation focuses on three NASA POWER environmental variables. Its coarse geographic sampling limits detailed local-scale analysis, particularly for smaller countries and regions.

The machine-learning models identify unusual environmental observations but do not establish the causes of those anomalies or predict future disasters. Formal long-term trend significance testing remains an area for further development.

Future improvements could include higher-resolution satellite observations, MODIS vegetation indices, NASA FIRMS active-fire data, additional country-specific models, and statistical trend analysis using methods such as Mann–Kendall testing and Sen’s slope estimation.

Conclusion

Terra Signal demonstrates how NASA’s open Earth science data can be transformed into an interactive, intelligent, and accessible environmental analysis platform. By integrating historical observations, interpretable statistical methods, country-specific machine-learning models, and geographic visualization, the project enables users to investigate environmental variability and identify potentially significant anomalies.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between complex scientific datasets and practical environmental understanding, empowering more people to explore Earth system changes and make informed, data-driven decisions about our changing planet.
